name: Tara Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy paper, boxes, tape and bubble wrap for Eastgate Packaging, a distributor out past the ring road. I keep a paper ledger next to the computer, because I trust my own handwriting more than a screen. In the morning I phone the mills and box plants, and in the afternoon I haggle over freight. Twenty-nine years and I've never had a supplier I couldn't get on the phone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the haggling. I'm good at it and I know it. What wears me out is the computer system, which changes every year and always seems to remove the one button I used. My husband Ray drives a bread delivery van, so between us we're up at five most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing changes, leave me alone. I've seen three waves of the next big thing at Eastgate and each one mostly made more work. I'd say the same at the pub and at the family dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm still worried. Eastgate lost a big customer in the spring, and boxes are cheap, margins are thin. If the firm slips, I'm a 58-year-old woman with no savings and there's nothing else within an hour's drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, same as ever. I'd keep my paper ledger and my phone calls. I'd try to put 50 a month away, though last winter's heating bill ate it. And I'd keep an eye on whether the owner, Mr. Delacroix, starts talking about cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but I'm used to it. It's the background hum of my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ray's hours were cut. How did you and he decide what to give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray's van company cut his hours by a day a week last year, so we're down already. We cancelled the holiday and I stopped buying lunch at work. That kind of thing doesn't make headlines but it's what's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody in particular. Is there anyone you'd want to fix those basics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody in particular. It's the economy, it's supermarkets squeezing everybody, it's luck. I'm not one for blaming. I'd just like someone to fix the basics, like energy bills.

say: I'd say **nothing changes**, so leave me alone; I've seen three waves of hype already.
I'd say the real fix is **energy bills** and basics, not technology.
think: The firm lost a big customer, so I'm worried about **cuts** even in the quiet world.
With no savings and nothing nearby, losing this job would be **disaster**.
do: Keep my **paper ledger** and phone calls going as usual.
Try to put **50 a month** aside, though heating bills ate it last winter.
Watch for any talk of **cuts** from the owner.
feel: **Tense**, but used to it: it's the background hum of my life.
S0.quote: If the firm slips, I'm a 58-year-old woman with no savings and there's nothing else within an hour's drive.
fieldNote: Anxious even in the mildest world because the firm lost a **customer** and her husband's hours were cut.
Practical and unwilling to blame; pins problems on the economy and **supermarkets**.
Small details such as **cancelled** holidays show the real pressure.

steps.text: Keep phoning the mills and box plants every morning
Put 50 a month into a savings account
Skip the work lunch and bring food from home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. I've heard this before. But I'd also say the order screens are getting cleverer, and the girl in accounts says half her reports now write themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, it frightens me. Ordering is checking and pricing, and a computer can do that. The part I do best is haggling by phone, and I can't be sure that counts for much if the firm only wants the cheapest price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the phone calls and be the person who knows every supplier by voice. I wouldn't touch the AI stuff, because I don't trust it. I'd cut our budget by 150 a month. And I'd ask Ray's boss if there's a second route for him, in case my pay goes down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. Like waiting for a test result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Dennis. What did you notice and what did you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I saw it with Dennis, our stock clerk. The firm put in the scanner system and Dennis wasn't replaced when he left. Nobody said anything, they just stopped advertising the job. That's how I'd expect it to go for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't touch the AI tools. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the owners will do what they have to. I don't blame them. If the competitor uses the software and we don't, we're finished. It's just that the people at the bottom pay.

say: I'd say **we'll see**, because I've heard this before, but the order screens are getting cleverer.
I'd say owners do what they must: if rivals use the software, we're **finished**.
think: It frightens me: ordering is checking and pricing, and a **computer** can do that.
My haggling by phone may not count if the firm only wants the **cheapest** price.
do: Be the person who knows every supplier by **voice** and keep the calls going.
Cut the household budget by **150 a month**.
Ask Ray's boss about a **second route** for his work.
feel: **Uncomfortable**, like waiting for a test result.
S1.quote: The firm put in the scanner system and Dennis wasn't replaced when he left. Nobody said anything, they just stopped advertising the job.
fieldNote: Sees the pattern of leaving jobs **unfilled**, so she expects quiet cuts.
**Refuses** AI tools because she doesn't trust them, which limits her options.
Doesn't blame owners; blames the market **squeezing** the bottom.

steps.text: Keep phoning the key mills in person every week
Cut the household budget by 150 a month
Ask Ray's boss about adding a second delivery route

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's ridiculous, then I'd go home and not sleep. Two years. Nobody can get ready for that, least of all a firm like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm gone. Not on day one, but inside the year. Ordering and pricing is what the machine does best. I'd be 60 with a husband whose van company is also shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Mr. Delacroix and ask what the plan is. I'd ask about severance in writing. I'd apply for anything hands-on that's local, like picking and packing in our own warehouse, since robots are three years behind. I'd cut everything we can and sell my mother's old ring. And I'd talk to my sister about moving in with her if it comes to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Not dramatic scared. Just a cold, flat feeling in the stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask about severance in writing. What do you expect them to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Aidan he's on his own with his rent and that we can't help. That's the hardest thing I can imagine saying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that conversation with your son Aidan sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone should have seen it coming and made rules. But they won't, and in my experience it's the ordinary person who ends up paying. I'd be angry at everyone and no one, which isn't helpful.

say: I'd say it's **ridiculous**, then go home and not sleep; nobody can prepare in two years.
I'd ask the owner for **severance** in writing.
think: I think I'm **gone** inside the year, because ordering and pricing is what the machine does best.
At 60 I'd have a husband whose **van company** is shaky too.
do: Ask Mr. Delacroix what the **plan** is for buyers.
Apply for hands-on **picking and packing** work in our warehouse.
Sell my mother's old **ring** and move in with my sister if needed.
feel: **Scared**, in a cold, flat way rather than a dramatic one.
S2.quote: I'd tell my son Aidan he's on his own with his rent and that we can't help. That's the hardest thing I can imagine saying.
fieldNote: Expects to lose her job and her husband's work is shaky, so alarmed, but stays **practical**.
Hands-on **warehouse** work is her chosen fallback because robots come later.
**Family** strain is clear: she can't help her son with his rent.

steps.text: Ask Mr. Delacroix for the buyers' severance terms in writing
Apply for picking and packing work in our own warehouse
Sell my mother's old ring to build a cushion
Move in with my sister if the job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit better, but only a bit. I'd tell the girls in accounts to keep their eyes open and not trust a promise from the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63. I think I could hold on until then if I'm quiet and useful. Retirement at 65 is the target. So it's two years short, and that's where it gets tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work as much as they let me and save every spare penny. I'd aim for 200 a month, even if that means no more meals out. I'd sell the second car and use Ray's van for errands. And I'd try to learn the new system just well enough not to be the one who breaks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit less scared than the 2028 one. But the dread is always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the two-year gap you mentioned. What would you do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ray not to count on a long retirement. We'd need to downsize and maybe move closer to my sister. It sounds sad, but I'd rather say it now than in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an early package? What would be a fair one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably retire early if the firm offered a package. I don't want to leave, but I wouldn't turn money down.

say: I'd tell colleagues to keep their eyes open and not trust **promises** from the top.
I'd say five years is **better**, but only a bit.
think: I could hold on until **63** if I stay quiet and useful, but retirement at 65 is two years away.
The dread is always there, even if it's less than the 2028 case.
do: Save **200 a month**, giving up meals out.
Sell the **second car** and use Ray's van for errands.
Learn the new system just well enough not to be the one who **breaks it**.
feel: **Less scared** than in the two-year world, but the dread stays.
S3.quote: I'd work as much as they let me and save every spare penny. I'd aim for 200 a month, even if that means no more meals out.
fieldNote: Five years leaves a two-year gap to **retirement**, so she still sees real risk.
Plans a **downsized** life and would accept a package.
Her small, **concrete** savings steps show control.

steps.text: Save 200 a month by giving up meals out
Sell the second car and share Ray's van
Ask the owner about an early retirement package
Learn the new ordering system well enough to avoid mistakes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say fine, I'll be retired. I'd say to the younger ones that they should worry, not me. And I'd say they'd better learn to do something with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 and retired. So my own work isn't at risk. It's my children and the price of everything that bother me. If AI makes things cheaper, perhaps it helps. If not, it's pensions and a smaller house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 65 and then stop. I'd get the mortgage down and put the rest into a pension top-up, around 150 a month. I'd tell my son Aidan to train as a plumber or an electrician, because those jobs are the last to go. And I'd stay out of whatever the firm does with its software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, I think. It's the first one where I think I'd be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hands-on work is the last to go. Where does that idea come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray and I would downsize. We'd live on the pension and what we've saved, and I'd keep working part-time if I could. It's not glamorous but it's solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask the government to protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the government to keep the state pension safe. That's the one thing I'd ask for. Not handouts. Just don't take it away.

say: I'd say the young ones should worry, not me, and they should **learn a trade**.
I'd say the government must keep the **state pension** safe.
think: At 68 I'd be **retired**, so my own work isn't at risk.
Cheaper goods from AI might help, but otherwise it's **pensions** and a smaller house.
do: Pay down the mortgage and put **150 a month** into a pension top-up.
Tell Aidan to train as a **plumber** or electrician.
feel: **Settled**: the first world where I think I'd be okay.
S4.quote: I'd tell my son Aidan to train as a plumber or an electrician, because those jobs are the last to go.
fieldNote: **Retirement** falls inside the window, so her own job isn't at stake, and she feels settled.
Advice to her son comes from **watching** hands-on work last longest.

steps.text: Pay 150 a month into a pension top-up
Tell Aidan to train as a plumber or electrician
Downsize to a smaller house near my sister

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years, no savings, a husband whose job is shaky too. What would help is plain: a proper severance package, a state pension that doesn't get cut, and the firm being straight with us. I don't want a handout. I want a warning I can plan around.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people like me aren't stupid for not using the new tools. I'm good at what I do. I just don't think anyone is going to ask me before they decide.

headlineQuote: I'm good at what I do. I just don't think anyone is going to ask me before they decide.
portrait: **Tara Quinn**, 58, buys paper and packaging for a distributor and keeps a paper ledger by the screen.
She is **centre** and resistant: she never uses AI, trusts the phone and refuses to blame anyone in particular.
Thin savings, a husband on shaky hours and few local jobs keep her **anxious** even when little changes.
She expects unfilled jobs and quiet cuts, and would fall back on warehouse work, her sister and selling things.
Her **calm** only appears in the ten-year world, when retirement falls inside the window.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because two years with no savings and a shaky household gives her no room.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **severance** package, a safe state pension and straight talk from the firm.
